nameStory: The Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite gets its name from its favorite host plant - black cherry trees - and its specialty of creating distinctive galls (abnormal growths) on the leaves. These tiny mites essentially hijack the plant's growth, causing it to form protective bumps and pockets where the mites live and feed.
description: This is an incredibly tiny mite that you'll never see with the naked eye, measuring less than 0.2mm long. Instead of spotting the mite itself, you'll notice their handiwork: small, rounded galls or blisters on black cherry leaves. These microscopic arachnids have elongated, worm-like bodies with just two pairs of legs (unlike most mites which have four pairs). They're so small that hundreds could fit on the head of a pin!

idTips.label: Gall Formation
idTips.description: Look for small, rounded bumps or blisters on black cherry leaves that feel firm and slightly raised when you run your finger over them

idTips.label: Host Plant
idTips.description: Always found on black cherry trees, which have distinctive serrated leaves with a glossy dark green surface and smooth bark with horizontal lines

idTips.label: Gall Texture
idTips.description: The galls feel slightly spongy when gently pressed and may have a small opening or appear sealed depending on the mite's life stage

idTips.label: Leaf Position
idTips.description: Galls typically appear on the upper surface of leaves, creating visible bumps that cast small shadows

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual galls are usually 2-5mm across, about the size of a small peppercorn, and may cluster together on heavily infested leaves

habitat: Found throughout New England wherever black cherry trees grow, from forest edges and woodlands to suburban areas and old fields. They prefer sunny to partially shaded locations where cherry trees thrive, typically in well-drained soils from sea level to mid-elevations.

seasonality.spring: Mites become active as cherry leaves emerge, beginning to form new galls that appear as small bumps on fresh foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak gall development occurs, with mature galls clearly visible as rounded bumps on cherry leaves throughout the canopy.
seasonality.fall: Galls may darken or dry out as leaves prepare to drop, with mites seeking overwintering sites in bark crevices.
seasonality.winter: Mites overwinter in protected locations on the tree, invisible until spring activity resumes with new leaf growth.

funFact: Cherry gall azure butterfly caterpillars actually feed on these galls and the mites inside them, making this one of the few cases where a butterfly depends entirely on microscopic arachnids for survival!
confusionNotes: The galls might be confused with fungal infections or other plant diseases, but gall mite bumps are typically more uniform and rounded than irregular fungal growths. If you see perfectly round, firm bumps on cherry leaves, think mites rather than disease.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly classified in the genus Phytoptus, so you may see it listed under that name in older field guides. Gall mites represent a fascinating example of how tiny creatures can dramatically alter plant structure for their own benefit.
compareHints: Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates elongated, finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that forms reddish blisters on fruit trees, the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite creates distinctly rounded, bump-like galls. Each Eriophyes species is highly host-specific, so the plant you find the galls on is your best identification clue.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red Nail Gall Mites create the most dramatically shaped galls in their genus - while relatives like the Lime Felt Gall Mite create fuzzy patches and others make simple bumps or blisters, only tiliae produces these unmistakable nail or horn-shaped protrusions.
Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates short, nail-like bumps on linden trees, the Plum Finger Gall Mite makes much longer, more cylindrical projections.

While many Eriophyes species create galls on different trees, the Alder Leaf Gall Mite's small, simple dome-shaped galls are quite different from relatives like the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that causes broad, blistered areas rather than distinct bumps.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-shaped galls on linden trees or finger-like projections on cherry leaves, the Birch Leaf Gall Mite creates relatively simple bumps and fuzzy patches.
Eriophyes rhoinus differs from its relatives primarily by its host plant preference for sumac species, while other Eriophyes mites specialize on different trees like cherry, maple, or alder.

While many Eriophyes mites in New England create galls on different trees, the Lime Felt Gall Mite is unique in producing that characteristic felt texture - its close relative the Red Nail Gall Mite makes hard, nail-like projections on linden leaves, while others like the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite create smooth pouches.
Unlike other Eriophyes species that target maples, cherries, or birches, this species is exclusively found on viburnums.
Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite that creates elongated finger-like projections, the Maple Gall Mite produces rounder, more dome-shaped galls.

Eriophyes leionotus differs from its relatives primarily by its specific host plant preferences and gall characteristics rather than the mite's appearance, since all Eriophyes species look remarkably similar under magnification.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-like projections (Red Nail Gall Mite) or finger-shaped growths (Plum Finger Gall Mite), the Serviceberry Gall Mite creates more subtle, pouch-like swellings.

Unlike other Eriophyes mites that create finger-like projections (like Plum Finger Gall Mite) or felt-like patches (like Lime Felt Gall Mite), the Pearleaf Blister Mite creates smooth, dome-shaped blisters.

Unlike its relatives that create felt-like patches (Lime Felt Gall Mite) or target fruit trees (Pearleaf Blister Mite), the lime gall mite creates distinct raised bumps specifically on basswood leaves.

Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite which creates smooth, nail-like projections, or the Lime Felt Gall Mite which makes dense, hair-like patches, this species creates more irregularly-shaped, moderately fuzzy galls.
